content: Ethoprim and trimethoprim both have the potential to prolong the QTc interval. Sulfamethoxazole can increase the levels or effects of trimethoprim through competition for renal tubular clearance, though this interaction is considered minor and of unknown clinical significance. Close monitoring is recommended. Similarly, trimipramine and trimethoprim, as well as trimipramine and sulfamethoxazole, can both prolong the QTc interval. Sulfamethoxazole may decrease trimipramine levels through an unspecified mechanism, which is also considered minor and of unknown significance, warranting close monitoring. Trimethoprim and tropisetron, as well as sulfamethoxazole and tropisetron, can both prolong the QTc interval. Caution and monitoring are advised. Trimethoprim can increase the levels or effects of tucatinib through mechanisms involving hepatic and intestinal enzyme CYP3A4 metabolism. This interaction is serious, and alternative drugs should be considered. Tucatinib can also increase trimethoprim levels via the same metabolic pathway. Concomitant use of tucatinib with CYP3A substrates should be avoided, as even minimal concentration changes can lead to severe or life-threatening toxicities. If unavoidable, the dose of the CYP3A substrate should be reduced per product labeling. Sulfamethoxazole and trimethoprim both decrease the efficacy of the live typhoid vaccine through pharmacodynamic antagonism, making their use contraindicated. Administration of live bacterial vaccines should be delayed until antibiotic therapy is completed. Valganciclovir may increase the toxicity of sulfamethoxazole through pharmacodynamic synergy, though the clinical significance is unclear, and close monitoring is advised. Sulfamethoxazole and valoctocogene roxaparvovec may both increase the risk of hepatotoxicity, necessitating caution and close monitoring. Alternative medications should be considered if potential drug interactions are identified. Valproic acid can increase sulfamethoxazole levels by affecting hepatic enzyme CYP2C9/10 metabolism, though the clinical significance is unclear. Close monitoring is recommended. Valsartan and trimethoprim both increase serum potassium levels, which may lead to hyperkalemia, particularly in patients with renal insufficiency or those on high doses. Monitoring is essential. Sulfamethoxazole and venlafaxine, as well as trimethoprim and venlafaxine, can both prolong the QTc interval, requiring caution and monitoring. Sulfamethoxazole and trimethoprim can increase verapamil levels through competition for renal tubular clearance, though the clinical significance is unclear. Sulfamethoxazole may increase phototoxicity when used with verteporfin due to pharmacodynamic synergy. Trimethoprim and voclosporin both decrease serum potassium levels, necessitating caution and monitoring. Trimethoprim and voriconazole, as well as sulfamethoxazole and voriconazole, can both prolong the QTc interval. Sulfamethoxazole and voriconazole can also increase each other's levels by affecting hepatic enzyme CYP2C9/10 metabolism. Close monitoring is advised. Sulfamethoxazole can increase warfarin levels by inhibiting CYP2C9 and through protein-binding displacement, potentially necessitating a 10-20% reduction in warfarin dosage. Willow bark may increase sulfamethoxazole levels through an unspecified mechanism, though the clinical significance is unclear. Zafirlukast can increase sulfamethoxazole levels by affecting CYP2C9/10 metabolism. Trimethoprim and sulfamethoxazole both increase zidovudine levels by decreasing renal clearance, and zidovudine may increase sulfamethoxazole toxicity through pharmacodynamic synergy. Close monitoring is recommended. Sulfamethoxazole and ziprasidone, as well as trimethoprim and ziprasidone, can both prolong the QTc interval, requiring therapy modification and close monitoring. Adverse effects associated with sulfamethoxazole and trimethoprim include anorexia, nausea, vomiting, vertigo, seizures, peripheral neuritis, erythema multiforme, hyperkalemia, rash, urticaria, immune hypersensitivity reactions, Stevens-Johnson syndrome, toxic epidermal necrolysis, agranulocytosis, aplastic anemia, hyponatremia, hematopoietic disorders, fulminant hepatic necrosis, thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura, idiopathic thrombocytopenic purpura, QT prolongation leading to ventricular tachycardia and torsades de pointes, embryo-fetal toxicity, and hypersensitivity reactions. Severe pulmonary adverse reactions, including acute respiratory failure and interstitial lung disease, have been reported. Renal complications such as interstitial nephritis, elevated BUN and creatinine, renal insufficiency, oliguria, anuria, crystalluria, and nephrotoxicity may occur, particularly in association with cyclosporine. Contraindications include known hypersensitivity, age under 2 months, severe renal impairment (CrCl <15 mL/min) when renal function cannot be monitored, documented megaloblastic or folate deficiency anemia, significant hepatic impairment, pregnancy at term, and nursing mothers due to the risk of kernicterus. Sulfonamides should not be used to treat group A beta-hemolytic streptococcal infections, as they do not eradicate the bacteria or prevent rheumatic fever. Caution is advised in elderly patients, those with impaired renal or hepatic function, folate deficiency, severe allergies, or bronchial asthma. Patients receiving high doses for Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia (PJP) should be monitored for propylene glycol toxicity and acid-base disturbances. Therapy should be discontinued at the first sign of serious adverse reactions, such as rash, fever, or hematologic changes. Prolonged use may result in fungal or bacterial superinfection. Sulfonamides may precipitate porphyria crises and hypothyroidism, and caution is advised in patients with porphyria or thyroid dysfunction. Hematologic changes indicative of folic acid deficiency may occur, particularly in elderly patients or those with preexisting folate deficiency, and are reversible with folinic acid therapy. Trimethoprim may impair phenylalanine metabolism, though this is not clinically significant in phenylketonuric patients on appropriate dietary restrictions. Severe cases of immune-mediated thrombocytopenia have been reported, resolving within a week of discontinuation. Co-administration with leucovorin for PJP treatment in HIV-positive patients has been associated with treatment failure and excess mortality and should be avoided. Sulfamethoxazole and trimethoprim therapy during pregnancy should only be used if the potential benefit justifies the risk to the fetus. Breastfeeding is not recommended during therapy due to the risk of bilirubin displacement and kernicterus in the infant.
